title: the word Pope Francis kept saying
hookLine: the word Pope Francis kept saying

lines: A POPE WHO RODE THE BUS.
A SINNER THE LORD LOOKED UPON.
cards: In 2013, a man from Buenos Aires who used to ride the bus to work became pope and took a name no pope had ever used: Francis, after the saint from Assisi you met yesterday.
One word kept coming up, in sermons, in interviews, off the cuff to crowds. He called a whole year after it. He titled a book after it.
Asked once, early on, to describe himself, he said, in effect: a sinner the Lord has looked upon. Pope Francis led the Church until his death in 2025. Today, his word: mercy.

teach.h: MISERICORDIA — A HEART FOR THE WRETCHED.
teach.b: The Latin word is misericordia. Inside it are two smaller words: miser, wretched, in trouble, and cor, the heart. Mercy is a heart that goes out to someone in misery.
Not a verdict. A heart. The Bible's Hebrew has a word for it that comes from the word for a mother's womb, the kind of love you feel for a child you carried.
Luke's Gospel puts it at the center of what Jesus asks, in the Douay-Rheims Bible: "Be ye therefore merciful, as your Father also is merciful."

Pope Francis took his motto from an old sermon by Bede, an English monk, about the day Jesus called Matthew, a tax collector everyone despised. Jesus looked at him, Bede says, with mercy, and chose him.

teach.h: BY HAVING MERCY, AND BY CHOOSING.
teach.b: By having mercy, and by choosing. Francis said that was his own story. That's where today's line comes from.
Francis kept saying that people who can't show mercy have often never let themselves receive it.

teach.h: YOU CAN'T GIVE WHAT YOU WERE NEVER HANDED.
teach.b: You can't give away what you've never been handed.

So the first step is to accept it: to let God, or someone, look at you with mercy and choose you anyway, the way Jesus looked at Matthew. For some people, the hardest one to show mercy to is themselves.
Then it flows outward: forgiving, feeding, visiting, going toward people in trouble. Catholics call these the works of mercy. Francis of Assisi kissing the leper's hand was the same heart.
And confession, from day three, is the Church saying it out loud: you're forgiven.

how: Catholics practice the corporal and spiritual works of mercy, such as feeding the hungry, visiting the sick and forgiving injuries, and celebrate Divine Mercy Sunday on the Sunday after Easter.

games.q: what's inside the word — tap the pairs.

the tax collector looked upon and chosen

s: mercy comes from Latin words for heart and the wretched
misericordia: a heart that goes out to someone in misery.
Pope Francis's motto was taken from Bede, an English monk
miserando atque eligendo, from Bede's sermon on the call of Matthew.
mercy means pretending something bad didn't happen
mercy looks straight at it, and the heart goes out anyway.

games.q: Jesus walks past Matthew, a tax collector the whole town despises, sitting at his booth. what happens, in Bede's telling?
o: he walks past without a glance.
he looks at him with mercy, and chooses him.
games.why: by having mercy, and by choosing: miserando atque eligendo. Pope Francis made it his motto.

practice: Here's the practice. Bring to mind one thing you haven't quite forgiven yourself for, if there is one. Something small is fine.
Picture someone who loves you looking at it, and at you, without flinching. Not excusing it. Just looking at you with a heart that goes out to you.
Breathe slowly, and let yourself be looked at like that. If you pray, you can let that look be God's.

wordCard.voice: Mercy. Misericordia: a heart that goes out to someone in trouble, received first, then given away. Eighteenth word.

orig.note: Latin: mercy. from miser, wretched, and cor, the heart.

carryVoice: Your line: start with yourself. Mercy received is the only kind you can pass on. Day eighteen.
